newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy grows strongly, but outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy grows strongly, but outlook cloudy.

text.p: Japan's economy grew strongly in the three months to the end of March as consumers rushed to buy goods ahead of an increase in the national sales tax, the government said on Friday.

The spurt in economic activity in the January-March quarter propelled overall growth in Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) well beyond the government's official target for the 1996/97 fiscal year of 2.5 percent.

GDP -- which measures total output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production -- rose a healthy 1.6 percent in the January-March quarter from the previous quarter, or an annualised 6.6 percent.

Growth was boosted by strong private consumption ahead of a rise in Japan's sales tax on April 1 from three to five percent. The GDP growth in the latest quarter compares with revised growth of 0.9 percent for the October-December quarter.

But economists said the brisk tempo of growth would not be enough to prompt a change in Japan's low interest rate policy, and predicted the pace may slow in the current quarter as the higher tax burden weighs on economic activity.

For fiscal 1996/97, GDP -- a closely watched pointer to the health of the economy -- rose a real 3.0 percent from the previous year after a revised figure of 2.4 percent growth in 1995/96, the government figures showed.

The figures for both quarterly and annual economic growth were at the top end of economists' forecasts, which had, on average, predicted that real GDP for the January-March period would grow 1.1 percent from the previous quarter. Their forecasts for GDP growth for the full fiscal year ranged from 2.7 percent to 3.0 percent.

"These are very good numbers. This is going to lead everyone to revise upward their (GDP) forecasts for the (1997) calendar year to 2.5 percent," said Kenneth Courtis, chief economist with Deutsche Bank Group Asia.
But economists also said although the data confirmed that the economy was steadily growing, the real focus is on the economy's performance in the months after the tax increase.

They said the prospect of higher taxes from April was the main engine for economic growth in the January-March period, as consumers rushed to buy goods before the rise, and added that the impact of the fiscal tightening will be felt in the period after April.

"I expect both spending and capital investment to slump in the April-June quarter in reaction to the surprisingly robust spending growth of an annualised 20 percent for the January-March quarter," said Yasushi Okada, deputy director of securities investment advisory department at Daiwa Securities.

The government admitted that growth in the January to March period was largely due to accelerated consumer demand ahead of the tax increase, but said the economy was still on track for this fiscal year's growth target.

"Even if there were a considerable deceleration in the April to June period, we can achieve the government's target of around 1.9 percent centring on domestic demand," Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya said.
Tokyo has set a target of 1.9 percent growth in GDP for the fiscal 1997/98 year.
But economists said the strong growth for the first three months of the year alone would not lead to a change in Japan's easy monetary policy.

"I don't believe we will have an ODR (official discount rate) hike anytime soon just because of this very historical piece of data, greatly influenced by consumption and other factors, has come out higher than expected," said Jane Berryman, senior analyst at Technical Data in Tokyo.
"The Bank of Japan is likely to hold on to its relaxed monetary policy until they examine data for July-September," added Daiwa's Okada.
